title: Co-brokering vs. double brokering: check the arrangement
seoTitle: Co-brokering vs. double brokering: check the arrangement
searchIntent: How should a broker evaluate a co-brokering arrangement?
excerpt: Trace the contracts, carrier selection, communication and payment responsibilities when another broker is involved.
takeaway: Before accepting a co-brokered load, establish who engaged each party, what the contracts permit, who selects the carrier and who pays. A label alone does not resolve the arrangement.

sections.title: Draw the contractual chain before discussing labels
paragraphs: In a straightforward brokerage movement, the shipper engages the broker and the broker arranges transportation with a carrier. Adding another brokerage introduces another relationship that must be understood.

Luis discusses working with another broker for specialized service or capacity. The useful starting point is not whether the arrangement has a reassuring label. Identify which business tenders the load, selects the carrier, issues instructions, invoices and pays.

sections.title: Put the division of work in writing
paragraphs: A co-broker agreement should address the specific relationship rather than leaving each side to assume the other is responsible. Discuss customer communication, carrier engagement, billing, payment and how problems will be handled.

Protection of customer and carrier relationships also needs explicit treatment. Have counsel review the actual arrangement and the applicable contracts. A signature alone does not establish that every planned activity is authorized or that every contractual risk has disappeared.

sections.title: Check that the documents describe the same movement
paragraphs: Compare the tender, rate confirmation, bill of lading and invoice trail. Determine who accepted the shipment and who is actually performing the transportation. A mismatch deserves investigation before the load proceeds.

Clear paperwork helps operations as well as collections. When delivery is delayed or an invoice is disputed, the team should not have to guess which party can issue instructions or which agreement governs the work.

sections.title: Separate agreement risk from credit risk
paragraphs: An agreement does not make a counterparty able to pay. Luis’s broader lesson about knowing the other business applies even when the relationship has been documented.

Evaluate the payment path and credit exposure independently. Understand whether your payment depends on another party collecting first and what happens if there is a dispute. Do not treat a written arrangement as a guarantee of recovery.

sections.title: Verify the legal and insurance details for your structure
paragraphs: FMCSA guidance distinguishes broker activities and bona fide agency relationships based on the work performed. Labels alone are not enough to resolve a particular arrangement.
Confirm authority, contract permissions and insurance with the appropriate professionals. The legal and insurance consequences depend on the actual activity, agreements and coverage.
